'''''Hesperoyucca whipplei''''' ([[syn.]] ''Yucca whipplei''), the '''chaparral yucca''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | ''Hesperoyucca whipplei'' | 452304 | accessdate = 28 June 2013}}</ref> '''our Lord's candle''',<ref name=GRIN/> '''Spanish bayonet''',<ref name=Thomas>{{cite book|author1=Thomas, John Hunter |author2=Dennis R. Parnell|title=Native Shrubs of the Sierra Nevada|url=https://archive.org/details/nativeshrubsofsi00thom|url-access=registration |access-date=28 June 2013|date=1 January 1974|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=978-0-520-02538-7|pages=[https://archive.org/details/nativeshrubsofsi00thom/page/17 17]–}}</ref> '''Quixote yucca'''<ref name=GRIN/> or '''foothill yucca''',<ref name="Basey1992">{{cite book|author1=Basey, Harold E. |author2= Basey, John M.|author3= Basey, Paul E.|title=Basey's Sierra Nevada textbook: a complete reference for the Sierra Nevada student|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vcBOAQAAIAAJ|access-date=28 June 2013|year=1992|publisher=Robin Works|isbn=978-0-9622418-0-2}}</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]] closely related to, and formerly usually included in, the genus ''[[Yucca]]''. It is native to southwest communities of North America.

==Description==
{{more citations|date=January 2022|section}}
[[Image:Yucca whipplei flower.JPG|thumb|Several flowers, hundreds of which comprise the inflorescence]]

It produces a stemless [[basal rosette]] cluster of long, rigid [[leaves]] which end in a sharp point.<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Dale |first=Nancy |title=Flowering Plants: The Santa Monica Mountains, Coastal and Chaparral Regions of Southern California |collaboration=Hollombe, David |publisher=[[California Native Plant Society]] |year=2000 |isbn=0-943460-40-9 |editor-last=Kitz |editor-first=Jo |edition=2nd |location=Sacramento, California |pages=23-24 |oclc=45956454 |orig-year=1986 |editor-last2=Hardie-Scott |editor-first2=Linda |editor-last3=Hartman |editor-first3=Steven Louis}}</ref> The leaves are {{Convert|20–90|cm|in|abbr=on|0}},<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/328/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |pages=328–329 |orig-date=1979}}</ref> rarely to {{Convert|125|cm|abbr=on}}, long and {{Convert|0.7–2|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} wide, and gray-green in color. The leaf edges are finely saw-toothed.

The single [[inflorescence]] grows extremely fast, and reaches {{Convert|0.9–3|m|ft|frac=2}} tall, bearing hundreds of elliptical (bell-shaped) white to purplish flowers {{Convert|3|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} in diameter on a densely branched [[panicle]] up to {{Convert|70|cm|abbr=on}} broad, covering the upper half of the inflorescence. The flowers are fragrant.<ref name=":7" /> The [[fruit]] is a dry winged [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]], which splits open at maturity to release the [[seed]]s. According to [[Guinness]] the [[inflorescence]] [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] of ''H. whipplei'' can grow up to {{cvt|25|cm}} a day towards an eventual height of {{cvt|3.65|m}}.<ref>{{cite book | editor= Craig Glenday | date= 2005 | title= Guinness World Records - 2006 | location= London | publisher= Guinness World Records Ltd. | page= 97 | isbn= 1-904994-02-4 }}</ref>

The plant takes several (usually 5+) years to reach maturity and flower, doing so in April–May,<ref name=":6" /> at which point it usually dies. Most [[subspecies]] produce offshoots from the base, so that although the parent plant flowers and dies, a cluster of clones around its base continue to grow and reproduce. It may also grow back from its base after much of its foliage has been scorched off by the wildfires that are frequent in its range.

==Taxonomy==
The taxonomy of ''H. whipplei'' is complex and controversial.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242101658 Flora of North America]</ref> ''[[Hesperoyucca]]'' was described as a genus by [[George Engelmann]] as long ago as 1892,<ref>[http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do;jsessionid=FE8D88F2BF307B6B7A907D77EAF82444?id=24346-1&back_page=%2Fipni%2FeditAdvPlantNameSearch.do%3Bjsessionid%3DFE8D88F2BF307B6B7A907D77EAF82444%3Ffind_infragenus%3D%26find_isAPNIRecord%3Dtrue%26find_geoUnit%3D%26find_includePublicationAuthors%3Dtrue%26find_addedSince%3D%26find_family%3D%26find_genus%3DHesperoyucca%26find_sortByFamily%3Dtrue%26find_isGCIRecord%3Dtrue%26find_infrafamily%3D%26find_rankToReturn%3Dall%26find_publicationTitle%3D%26find_authorAbbrev%3D%26find_infraspecies%3D%26find_includeBasionymAuthors%3Dtrue%26find_modifiedSince%3D%26find_isIKRecord%3Dtrue%26find_species%3D%26output_format%3Dnormal Information] at [[IPNI]]</ref> but it has taken recent [[DNA analysis]] to confirm that they are genetically distinct from ''[[Yucca]]''.<ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120718044940/http://www.agavaceae.com/botanik/pflanzen/botanzeige_scan_en.asp?gnr=220&scan=22190&cat=5&name=Hesperoyucca%C2%A0newberryi|title=Agavaceae.com – page includes a key to''Yucca'' and the three recognised species of ''Hesperoyucca''}}</ref><!--retrieved 12th Nov 2009-->

Among those botanists who have treated (or still treat) it as a species of ''Yucca'', six subspecies have been recognised;<ref>Hochstätter, Fritz (Hrsg.): '' Yucca (Agavaceae). Band 1 Dehiscent-fruited species in the Southwest and Midwest of the USA, Canada and Baja California'', self-published, 2000. {{ISBN|3-00-005946-6}}</ref><ref>Hochstätter, Fritz (Hrsg.): '' Yucca (Agavaceae). Band 2 Indehiscent-fruited species in the Southwest, Midwest and East of the USA'', self-published. 2002. {{ISBN|3-00-009008-8}}</ref><ref>Hochstätter, Fritz (Hrsg.): '' Yucca (Agavaceae). Band 3 Mexico '', self-published, 2004. {{ISBN|3-00-013124-8}}</ref> others have regarded them as [[Variety (botany)|varieties]].<ref>[https://plants.usda.gov/java/nameSearch?mode=Scientific+Name&keywordquery=Yucca+californica Information] at [[USDA]] [[Natural Resources Conservation Service|NRCS]] PLANTS database</ref>

Hochstätter's subspecies are:
* [[Yucca whipplei ssp. whipplei|''Yucca whipplei'' ssp. ''whipplei'']]
* [[Yucca whipplei ssp. caespitosa|''Yucca whipplei'' ssp. ''caespitosa'']]
* [[Yucca whipplei ssp. intermedia|''Yucca whipplei'' ssp. ''intermedia'']]
* [[Yucca whipplei ssp. percursa|''Yucca whipplei'' ssp. ''percursa'']]
* [[Yucca whipplei ssp. newberryi|''Yucca whipplei'' ssp. ''newberryi'']]
* [[Hesperoyucca peninsularis|''Yucca whipplei'' ssp. ''eremica'']]

The plant treated as the subspecies ''Y. whipplei'' subsp. ''newberryi'' has been shown to be genetically distinct, and is often treated as a distinct species, ''[[Hesperoyucca newberryi]]''. It is native further east, in [[Arizona]], and differs in the capsules being unwinged or with only slight wings.

=== Etymology ===
*"Yuca" is a native name for the unrelated [[Manihot]], a genus in the [[spurge family]].<ref name=":7" />
*''Yucca whipplei'' is named after [[Amiel Weeks Whipple]] (1818–1863), a surveyor who oversaw the [[Southern Pacific Railroad|Pacific Railroad]] Survey to [[Los Angeles]] in 1853.<ref name=":7" />
*The name '''our Lord's candle''' is derived from its huge, flame-shaped inflorescence.
*'''Spanish bayonet''' refers to the needle-sharp leaf tips which can cause discomfort to the unwary passer-by.

==Distribution==
It is native to [[southern California]] in the [[United States]] and [[Baja California]] in [[Mexico]],<ref name=":6" /> where it occurs mainly in [[chaparral]], [[coastal sage scrub]], and [[California oak woodland|oak woodland]] plant communities at altitudes of 0–{{Convert|2,500|m|abbr=off}}.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{cite web |title='''Hesperoyucca whipplei''' (Torr.) Baker ''chaparral yucca'' |url=http://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-calrecnum=9995 |access-date=2013-05-09 |publisher=Calflora}}</ref> ''Yucca whipplei'' grows on the rocky slopes and washes of the chaparral area of the [[Transverse Ranges|transverse mountains]] of Southern California up to approximately {{Convert|4000|ft|abbr=on|order=flip}} above mean sea level.<ref name=":4" />

This is the only species of the [[asparagus family]] naturally present in the [[Santa Monica Mountains]] of the transverse ranges.<ref name=":7" /> 

==Ecology==
It blooms beginning in April through July, blooming abundantly in chaparral and oak woodland up to {{Convert|2,500|ft|abbr=off}}.<ref name=":7" /> The shoots that bear flowers die after flowering, but produce offsets around the old roots.<ref name=":7" />[[File:Yucca plants 2019b.jpg|thumb|Several plants in flower in the [[San Gabriel Mountains]]]]

It is pollinated by the California [[Tegeticula|yucca moth]] (''[[Tegeticula maculata]]''), a relationship which has become a classic example of [[Mutualism (biology)|mutualism]]. The female yucca moth collects up to a dozen sacks of pollen grains called [[pollinia]] and forms them into a massive ball. The moth then flies to another plant and lands on the ovary of a flower. Standing with its head near the [[stigma (botany)|stigma]], the moth inserts its [[ovipositor]] into the ovary wall and lays a single [[Egg (biology)|egg]]. The moth then rubs its pollen mass against the [[central stigmatic depression]], ensuring [[pollination]]. The pollinated ovary will now produce many seeds, ensuring an ample food supply for the [[larva]]. Although many associations of ''Yucca'' and yucca moth exist, ''Tegeticula maculata'' and ''Hesperoyucca whipplei'' form an exclusive relationship.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.uoregon.edu/~udovic/research.html |title=Reports on ongoing research by Professor Dan Udovic |publisher=[[University of Oregon]] |access-date=2009-11-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080807155806/http://www.uoregon.edu/~udovic/research.html |archive-date=2008-08-07 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=":6" />

==Uses==
''Hesperoyucca whipplei'' is used in [[xeriscaping]] in [[Southern California]], but reportedly is difficult to grow outside of its native range (although it is widely available from specialist nurseries in the United Kingdom).<ref>{{Cite book |title=RHS Plant Finder 2009–2010 |year=2009 |publisher=[[Dorling Kindersley]] |isbn=978-1-4053-4176-9 |page=804 }}</ref> It is extremely drought tolerant and thrives in clay soils.

It has been used extensively by [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]].<ref>{{cite book |first=J. W. |last=Dole |author2=B. B. Rose |year=1996 |page=59 |title=Shrubs and Trees of the Southern California Coastal Regions and Mountains |publisher=Foot-loose Press}}</ref> Yucca species such as ''Y. whipplei'' have been documented to have been used as a fiber and food source by Native Americans in the [[Indigenous peoples of the North American Southwest|Southwest]] cultural region, prior to European settlement.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{cite book|last1=Bean|first1=L.J.|last2=Vane|first2=S.B|last3=Heizer|first3=R.F.|title=Handbook of North American Indians Volume 8|date=1978|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington D.C.|isbn=0874741882|edition=1st}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite book|title=Survival Skills of Native California|date=1999|publisher=Gibbs Smith|isbn=0879059214|edition=1st|location=Salt Lake City, UT|last1=Campbell|first1=P.D.}}</ref> [[Archaeological]] evidence shows that use of yucca species extends to approximately 5,000 years ago within groups such as the [[Serrano people|Serrano]] of the [[San Bernardino Mountains]] and [[San Gabriel Mountains]] of the transverse mountain ranges of Southern California, where the species grows on rocky slopes and washes in chaparrals.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> The seeds would be ground into flour.<ref name=":7" /> The Serrano harvested the hearts of the plant during the spring growing season.<ref name=":0" /> Harvested plants were chosen based on the growth of the stalk; the hearts were the preferred portion of the plant, and would be harvested before the stalk was fully developed. The heart contains the sugars stored to rapidly grow a stalk to flower, and become bitter as the stalk grows in height.<ref name=":5" /> The hearts would then be roasted in stone lined pits ([[earth oven]]) over several hours in a manner similar to that of [[agave]] species. Once cooked, the hearts would be removed and allowed to cool before eating. Uneaten portions could be dried for storage.<ref name=":5" /> Though slightly bitter, the stalk and flowers can be harvested and used as food sources as well. The stalks can be prepared roasted in a manner similar to the hearts, while the petals were often parboiled.<ref name=":5" />
 
The long leaves of species such as the ''Y. whipplei'' are made of strong fibers which can be pounded and scraped to expose long threads which run the length of the leaf.<ref name=":5">{{cite book|last1=Campbell|first1=P.D.|title=Survival Skills of Native California|date=1999|publisher=Gibbs Smith|location=Salt Lake City, UT|isbn=0879059214|edition=1st}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{cite book|last1=Munz|first1=P.A.|title=A California Flora|date=1973|publisher=University of California Press|location=Los Angeles, CA|isbn=0520024052|pages=[https://archive.org/details/californiafloras00phil/page/1360 1360–1361]|edition=Combined|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/californiafloras00phil/page/1360}}</ref> The leaves could be processed in many ways to remove the outer layer of leaf material which could be processed into threads and cords, used for [[basketry]], blankets, and sandals.<ref name=":0" /> Green leaves can be heated over coals or directly on flames to heat the leaves. Cooking the leaves removes some of the [[saponins]] and allows for easier scraping. [[Ethnographic]] accounts dating to 1938 describes the preparation of leaves for fibers as any one of the following: [[boiling]] or pit roasting of live leaves to be scraped clean or the pounding or soaking of dry leaves expose fibers.<ref name=":1">{{cite book|last1=Kowta|first1=Makota|title=The Sayles Complex|url=https://archive.org/details/saylescomplexlat0000kowt|url-access=registration|date=1969|publisher=The University of California Press|location=Berkeley CA|isbn=0520090055|edition=1st}}</ref> Shells or stone scrapers were often employed to remove outer leaf material from the fibers.<ref name=":1" /> Once exposed, these fibers were often soaked in water to soften fiber. The fibers could then be twisted into cordage, used as materials in a basket, woven into sandals, and for making nets.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":0" />
 
Other groups made use of different varieties of yucca species found throughout the American Southwest.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> Archaeological evidence shows use of ''Yucca shidigera'' (Mojave yucca) near the area of the [[Mexico–United States border]] dating as early as 5,000 years ago.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> Residues of yucca were found on some stone tools in a cave site in [[Texas]] indicate that yucca was used to secure stone tools to other materials.<ref name=":2">{{cite journal|last1=Sobolik|first1=K.D.|title=Lithic organic residue analysis: an example from the Southwestern Archaic|journal=Journal of Field Archaeology|date=1996|volume=23|issue=4|pages=461–469|doi=10.2307/530548|jstor=530548}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{cite journal|last1=Sutton|first1=M.Q.|last2=Yohe, II|first2=R.M.|title=Perishable Artifacts from Cave No. 5, Providence Mountains, California|journal=Journal of California and Great Basin Anthropology|date=1988|volume=10|issue=1|pages=117–123}}</ref> Ethnographic evidence of the [[Mogollon culture|Mogollon]] has shown the use of the leaves with green leaf matter intact and woven into sandals.<ref name=":0" /> The green leaves are fire heated and no scraping or further processing occurs to remove fibers, though the spine is removed from the tip. The whole green leaves are then tightly woven to shape the bed of the sandal, and secured to the foot with cordage ties.<ref name=":0" />
